concepts.title: Slides lock speakers into a fixed order
concepts.summary: A slide deck is a sequence decided before the talk begins, so the speaker follows it even when the room wants to go somewhere else.
speechExamples: So here's the problem with slides: the order is locked in before you even start talking.
Someone asks about an earlier point and you end up clicking backwards through the whole deck.
The moment your explanation wanders off in a different direction, the slides are out of step with what you are saying.
Every time you stop to fiddle with the clicker, the audience loses the thread.
It ends up looking like the speaker is serving the slides instead of the other way round.
Think about how awkward it is when the conversation wants to go somewhere your deck doesn't.

sources.quote: Slides lock speakers into a fixed order
A slide deck is a sequence decided before the talk begins.
The audience sees the speaker serving the slides, instead of the slides serving the speaker.

concepts.title: The speech decides what the audience sees
concepts.summary: FOLLOW removes the slide sequence. The speaker prepares material once, explains it in any order, and the canvas follows the speech.
speechExamples: What FOLLOW does is flip that around, so the presentation follows me instead of me following it.
There is no slide order any more; I just explain things in whatever order makes sense.
You prepare your material once and then you simply talk, and the visuals form around what you say.
The speech itself decides what the audience gets to see.
I can answer a question, go back to an earlier idea, or change direction, and the visuals keep up.
The speaker leads, and the presentation follows.

sources.quote: The speech decides what the audience sees
FOLLOW removes the slide sequence entirely. The speaker prepares source material once, then explains it naturally in any order.
Usually, speakers follow their slides. With FOLLOW, the presentation follows the speaker.
The speaker leads. The presentation follows.

concepts.title: Four steps: capture, understand, match, compose
concepts.summary: Speech is captured, turned into text, matched to a prepared concept and composed on the canvas, continuously while the speaker talks.
speechExamples: Let me walk you through how it actually works, it's four steps.
First it listens to me through the laptop microphone.
Then the speech gets turned into text, right here on the device.
Next it compares the meaning of what I just said with the concepts we prepared from the document.
And finally it lays out the matching idea, its details and its connections on the canvas.
All four of those steps keep running the whole time I am talking.

concepts.title: Matching by meaning, and holding when unsure
concepts.summary: FOLLOW matches meaning rather than exact keywords. When it is not confident it holds the current view, and the speaker can always override it.
speechExamples: It isn't looking for keywords, it's matching on what I actually mean.
I don't have to recite a script; I can say things in my own words.
If it is not sure what I am talking about, it just stays where it is rather than guessing.
Umms, pauses and random asides like this one shouldn't move anything on screen.
And I'm always in control: one key press and my manual choice wins.
A late automatic decision can never override something I chose by hand.

sources.quote: Matching by meaning, and holding when unsure

concepts.title: Fixed slides compared with a speech-directed canvas
concepts.summary: Order, format, control and questions: decided in advance with fixed slides, decided by the speech with the FOLLOW canvas.
aliases: fixed slides compared with the canvas
speechExamples: If you put fixed slides side by side with what we're doing, the difference is pretty stark.
With slides the order is fixed before the talk, whereas here the speech decides it.
Compared with a deck of separate pages, this is one continuous canvas.
A clicker versus your own voice, with a manual override if you need it.
Slides make you search back for an earlier point, whereas FOLLOW just returns to it with its context.

concepts.title: Prepared once with AI, presented live on the device
concepts.summary: Before the talk an AI model proposes concepts linked to their pages, and the speaker approves them. During the talk, speech and matching run locally.
aliases: no audio sent to a server
speechExamples: So what happens before the talk? An AI model reads the document once and proposes the concepts.
Every concept and fact it suggests is linked back to the page it came from.
I review all of that and approve it before I ever present.
During the talk, the speech recognition and the matching run locally on this laptop.
To answer the privacy question: my live audio never gets sent to a server.
It only ever shows material I approved, it never makes up new facts on stage.
